subject: physics_2
question_text: Three capacitors of capacitances 1 μF, 2 μF and 3 μF are connected in series. (a) What is the ratio of charges? (b) What is the ratio of potential differences?

verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Two structural checks are IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the two-book union check (the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only) and the past-paper back-test (the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers). Hand-checked rather than copied: V ∝ 1/C gives 1 : 1/2 : 1/3; multiplying by 6 gives 6 : 3 : 2 — the book's printed ratio is arithmetically correct (check: 6+3+2 shares in proportion, and 1×6 = 2×3 = 3×2, equal Q = CV products).

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Ratio of charges
lines: (a) In series the same charge Q appears on
each capacitor, passed along plate to plate:
steps.margin_note: First mark. In series the charge is common by connection.
steps.why: The plate joining two neighbouring capacitors is an isolated section of conductor; the charge that appears on one face is drawn from the other, so every capacitor in the line carries the same Q.
common_mistakes: Writing 1 : 2 : 3 here — that is the PARALLEL charge ratio.

recall.must_convey: That in series the charge on every capacitor is the same, ratio one to one to one.
reject: V proportional to one by C

steps.memory_tip: Series is one line of charge — the same Q passes through every capacitor.

steps.label: Ratio of potential differences
lines: (b) V = Q/C, and Q is common, so V ∝ 1/C:
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The smallest capacitance takes the largest share of V.
steps.why: With the same Q on each, the capacitor that stores least charge per volt needs the most volts — so the 1 μF capacitor takes the biggest potential difference. Check: 1×6 = 2×3 = 3×2, the same Q = CV on each.
common_mistakes: Writing 1 : 2 : 3 for the potential differences — V goes as 1/C, not as C.
Clearing the fractions wrongly. 1 : 1/2 : 1/3 times 6 is 6 : 3 : 2.

recall.must_convey: That V is proportional to 1 by C, giving six to three to two.
accept: V proportional to one by C
smallest capacitor takes the most voltage

steps.memory_tip: Invert 1, 2, 3 and clear the fractions: 6, 3, 2. Smallest C, largest V.

insider_note: The check line 1×6 = 2×3 = 3×2 proves the ratio in one glance — each product is the same charge Q.
